stories.title: LIV Golf Financial Crisis — Saudi PIF Ends Funding — NEW

x_posts.label: Post 1-1
x_posts.text:
LIV Golf's Saudi funding is ending after 2026.

The fallout: Indianapolis prize money halved ($20M → $10.1M). Michigan finale cancelled. ~$60M in promised money gone.

A production company is suing for $1.23M in missed payments.

Players are still waiting for checks.

#LIVGolf

x_posts.label: Post 1-2
x_posts.text:
LIV Golf winner's purse at Indianapolis: $2.02M.

At every prior LIV event? $4M.

Saudi Arabia's PIF is pulling funding after this season. The numbers tell the story.

#LIVGolf

facebook.long_form:
Window: 8:00 AM ET

The LIV Golf experiment is ending — and the financial collapse is happening out in the open.

Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund announced in April that it would end its funding of LIV Golf after this 2026 season. What has followed is a cascade of consequences that have fundamentally changed the product players signed up for:

The Michigan Team Championship — which was supposed to be LIV's season-closing finale — has been cancelled entirely.

The Indianapolis individual purse has been cut in half: from $20 million to $10.1 million. The winner will earn $2.02 million — down from the $4 million prize that was standard at every prior LIV event.

The team championship prize pool at Indianapolis: $30 million total, with the winning team bonus cut from $11.2 million to $8.4 million.

In total, LIV players and teams have lost approximately $60 million in promised prize money across 2026, including the cancelled June Louisiana event.

And then there's the lawsuit. Fresh Tape Media — a production company that managed logistics and on-site production for LIV's January preseason event in West Palm Beach — filed a $1.23 million suit in New York Supreme Court in July, alleging more than $1 million in missed payments and interest. Players are also reportedly waiting for owed payments.

LIV launched with Saudi billions and the promise of a rival league that would pay players at levels the PGA Tour couldn't match. As the funding dries up, the gap between that promise and reality has become one of the defining stories of professional golf's turbulent 2026.

---

stories.title: Sepp Straka Withdraws From BMW Championship — NEW

x_posts.label: Post 2-1
x_posts.text:
Breaking: Sepp Straka withdraws from the BMW Championship.

The No. 5 FedExCup player is citing a private family matter and will not play at Bellerive.

He still plans to compete at the Tour Championship at East Lake.

The BMW field drops to 49 players.

#PGATour

x_posts.label: Post 2-2
x_posts.text:
Straka's BMW withdrawal means the bubble math for East Lake just shifted.

He was No. 5 in FedExCup. Players ranked 28-30 now have one fewer top-10 guy taking points away.

Some Tour Championship dreams got a little easier today.

#PGATour #BMWChampionship

facebook.long_form:
Window: 10:00 AM ET

Sepp Straka will not play in the BMW Championship at Bellerive Country Club this week.

The Austrian golfer — ranked No. 5 in the FedExCup standings heading into the playoffs — withdrew Tuesday citing a private family matter. His manager, Butler Melnyk, issued a statement requesting that the family's privacy be respected during this time. Straka is still expected to compete at the Tour Championship at East Lake in Atlanta next week.

The announcement carries real playoff implications. Straka was not just any player at No. 5 — he was one of the most secure qualifiers in the field, and his absence drops the BMW field from 50 to 49 players. The Tour does not fill the vacancy.

The consequence that will dominate leaderboard conversation this week: the top-30 cutoff bubble has shifted. Players sitting in positions 28, 29, and 30 are quietly recalculating. With Straka's substantial points production removed from the equation, the path to East Lake got marginally easier for some of the most stressed golfers in the field.

The human story is easy to appreciate — a professional athlete choosing family over a $20 million event is a decision that requires no defense. But in a sport where FedExCup positioning can define careers and earnings in outsized ways, Straka's withdrawal is a news event that reshapes the week's competitive narrative before a ball has been struck.

Watch the bubble. It moves.

---

stories.title: McIlroy at BMW — Two-Time Masters Champion Seeks Playoff Run — FOLLOW UP

x_posts.label: Post 3
x_posts.text:
Rory McIlroy heads to BMW as a two-time defending Masters champion.

2025: career Grand Slam.
2026: first back-to-back since Tiger.

He's ranked No. 13 in FedExCup after going 66th at St. Jude.

The greatest active golfer has work to do.

#PGATour

facebook.long_form:
Window: 10:00 AM ET

Rory McIlroy arrives at Bellerive Country Club this week as arguably the most accomplished active golfer in the world — and he knows his game is not where it needs to be.

The resume is extraordinary. In April 2025, McIlroy completed his career Grand Slam at Augusta National, ending an 11-year wait since his 2014 Open Championship and beating Bryson DeChambeau in a playoff. Then he went back to Augusta in April 2026 and won again — defending his Masters title, holding off Scottie Scheffler by one stroke despite surrendering a six-shot lead in the third round. McIlroy became the first player to win back-to-back Masters titles since Tiger Woods won in 2001 and 2002. He is only the fourth man to accomplish it in Masters history.

But after the Masters high, 2026 has been uneven. At the FedEx St. Jude Championship, McIlroy finished 66th at 8-over par — zero sub-par rounds across four days of competitive golf. He flew home to South Florida to work on his swing with longtime coach Michael Bannon. His own assessment of where his game stands: "far away from where I need to be."

He enters Bellerive at No. 13 in the FedExCup standings. East Lake is well within reach — but the margin for error is thin, and the BMW field is deep. He sits at +1600 in the odds, second only to Scheffler, reflecting both his talent and the recognition that talent and current form are not the same thing right now.

Three FedExCup titles. A career Grand Slam. Back-to-back Masters. And he's working on his swing this week at one of America's most storied golf venues.

This is what elite athletic careers look like at the top: never settled.

---

stories.title: CPKC Women's Open Opens Tomorrow — FOLLOW UP

x_posts.label: Post 4
x_posts.text:
CPKC Women's Open begins tomorrow at Royal Mayfair in Edmonton.

Nelly Korda (World No. 1) is the favorite. Brooke Henderson (defending champ, won at -15 in 2025) gets the hometown crowd.

Lydia Ko is chasing a 4th title — her first win here came at age 15.

#LPGA #CPKC

facebook.long_form:
Window: 8:00 AM ET

Today is pro-am day in Edmonton. Tomorrow, the world's best women golfers tee it up for real.

The 52nd CPKC Women's Open opens Round 1 at Royal Mayfair Golf Club on August 20 — and the 156-player field assembled on this Stanley Thompson-designed par 70 (6,452 yards) is one of the strongest on the LPGA calendar.

Nelly Korda headlines as World No. 1. She won four events in 2026, including three majors — the Chevron, the Riviera May Open, and the U.S. Women's Open. She has been the dominant force in women's golf this season and she arrives in Edmonton as the prohibitive favorite.

Brooke Henderson enters as the defending champion. Her 2025 title defense will be remembered: she shot a final-round 67 to close at -15 and beat Minjee Lee by a single stroke, earning her 14th LPGA title to become the winningest Canadian golfer in LPGA history. The Alberta crowd made clear then — and will make clear again tomorrow — what Henderson means to Canadian golf.

Lydia Ko has her own Royal Mayfair story. Ko won here in 2013 at the age of 15, as an amateur, becoming the youngest LPGA winner in history. She returned to win twice more. A fourth title at this course would be one of the more remarkable individual relationships between a golfer and a single venue in modern tour history.

Also in the field: Hyo Joo Kim, Miyu Yamashita, Ruoning Yin, Minjee Lee, and Hannah Green.

Round 1 begins tomorrow morning. The course is ready. The storylines are already written.

stories.title: LIV Indianapolis Season Finale Update — Perez Out, Rottluff In — FOLLOW UP

x_posts.label: Post 5
x_posts.text:
Victor Perez withdrew from LIV Indianapolis. His second child is arriving.

Max Rottluff of Germany steps in as his replacement.

Indianapolis is now LIV's only finale. Michigan was cancelled.

4Aces leads Ripper GC by 2.25 points with everything on the line.

#LIVGolf

facebook.long_form:
Window: 1:00 PM ET

Two days before the first shot is struck at The Club at Chatham Hills, LIV Golf's Indianapolis season finale has already absorbed its first lineup change.

Victor Perez — the Cleeks GC player who has been a consistent LIV presence through the 2026 season — withdrew from Indianapolis to be present for the birth of his second child. Germany's Max Rottluff steps in as his replacement. Perez sits well clear of LIV's relegation zone, so his withdrawal has no individual standing implications — but his absence is a reminder that athletes are human beings first.

The event itself carries unusual weight this year. When Saudi Arabia's PIF announced it was ending its LIV funding, the Michigan Team Championship — which was scheduled after Indianapolis — was cancelled. That means Indianapolis is now LIV's sole season finale: the place where the team championship, one of the tour's central competitive attractions, will be decided.

And the standings could hardly be closer. 4Aces GC (Dustin Johnson, Thomas Pieters, Thomas Detry, Anthony Kim) leads Ripper GC (Cameron Smith, Marc Leishman, Lucas Herbert, Elvis Smylie) by just 2.25 points in the team standings. Legion XIII is also within striking distance at third.

In the individual standings, Jon Rahm's title is already clinched — his third consecutive LIV individual championship — with Bryson DeChambeau in second at 726.20 points. The 72-hole, shotgun-start format begins Thursday.

Thomas Rhett performs Friday. Disco Lines Saturday. And the team championship gets settled somewhere in between.

---
